input:
In this worked example, the vapour pressure of ethanol at 40 °C is estimated by means of the Antoine equation, a widely used correlation that relates the vapour pressure of a pure liquid to temperature through three empirically fitted constants. The equation takes the following form:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

where $P$ denotes the vapour pressure and $T$ denotes the temperature. For ethanol, the constants in question are $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89, and $C$ = 230.3, with the pressure expressed in mmHg and the temperature in °C, and each constant plays its own distinctive role within the correlation, with $A$ effectively setting the level of the curve, $B$ governing the strength of the temperature dependence, and $C$ shifting the temperature scale in such a way that the curve is able to follow the measured data. Substituting $T$ = 40 into the equation and evaluating the right-hand side yields a vapour pressure of 133.5 mmHg, which, when converted into kilopascals, gives a final estimate of 17.8 kPa. It is important to note that this estimate is only as reliable as the fit on which it is based, since the constants are valid solely over the temperature range to which they were originally fitted, and an evaluation performed outside that range will still return a number, albeit one that carries no real standing. For design purposes, it is the source databank value that governs, and the Antoine estimate should properly be regarded as a convenient check on that value rather than as a substitute for it. Overall, the vapour pressure of ethanol at the temperature considered here, on the basis of the constants set out above, comes to 17.8 kPa, a figure that illustrates the usefulness of the correlation for rapid estimation while simultaneously underscoring the need to respect the limits within which the fitted constants can legitimately be applied.
target:
Estimate the vapour pressure of ethanol at 40 °C from the Antoine equation. The Antoine equation relates the vapour pressure of a pure liquid to temperature through three constants fitted to measured data:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

where $P$ denotes the vapour pressure and $T$ denotes the temperature. For ethanol, the constants are $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89, and $C$ = 230.3, with the pressure in mmHg and the temperature in °C. The constants divide the work between them: $A$ sets the level of the curve, $B$ carries the strength of the temperature dependence, and $C$ shifts the temperature scale so that the curve follows the measured pressures across the fitted range. The logarithm form is what makes the fit usable: vapour pressure climbs steeply with temperature, and the equation straightens that climb into a form three constants can hold. Substitution of $T$ = 40 into the equation gives a vapour pressure of 133.5 mmHg, and conversion to kilopascals gives 17.8 kPa. The estimate is a fit value, and it holds only where the fit holds. The constants are valid over their fitted temperature range, and the stated temperature must lie inside that range for the estimate to mean anything. Outside the range the equation still returns a number, and the number has no standing. The source databank value governs design. The Antoine estimate checks the databank value and does not replace it; where the two disagree by more than the scatter of the fit, the databank value stands and the estimate is set aside. A check of the direction is also available from the equation itself: the subtracted term shrinks as the temperature rises, so the calculated pressure rises with temperature, as a vapour pressure must. The vapour pressure of ethanol at the stated temperature, on the stated constants, is 17.8 kPa.
